label: L1
title: Introduction and Key Concepts and Frameworks for the Course
brief: Class 1 frames the course: the AI revolution mainstreams advanced analytics/AI models and shifts value toward data, but a model alone does not create value; what stands between analytics and impact is a change in mindset and representations. The electricity analogy carries the argument: Edison sold electricity from 1881, yet by 1900 less than 5% of US factory drive power came from electric motors, because value came only once factories reorganized around the new technology instead of swapping motors into steam-era layouts. Data creates value in two ways: data for products/services (improving today's business model) and products/services for data (new products, services and business models). The class builds a vocabulary for knowledge (Ackoff's data-to-wisdom hierarchy, Hausmann's tools/explicit/tacit productive knowledge, Schein's culture iceberg, Nonaka's knowledge creation) and an economic backdrop: AI as a general-purpose technology growing exponentially while organizations change linearly, intangibles rising to 92% of S&P 500 market value, and an AI investment cycle in which suppliers finance their own demand, as Cisco did before the dot-com crash. With models becoming a commodity, value moves to deployment, which favors T-shaped professionals who pair analytics depth with breadth in strategy, business model, operating model and change management.
kp: Key message: a model alone does not guarantee value; impact requires a change in mindset/representations, as with electricity a century ago.
Data creates value two ways: data for products/services (improve today's business model) and products/services for data (new products, services, business models).
Ackoff: data (symbols) → information (who/what/when/where/how many) → knowledge (how to) → understanding (why) → wisdom (which ends are worth pursuing).
Hausmann: productive knowledge = tools, explicit knowledge (codes, manuals, formulas, algorithms; transferable instantly at zero cost) and tacit know-how (hard to transfer).
Mindset = a coherent configuration of assumptions and beliefs that condition decisions, actions and behaviors; it sits in the tacit part of Schein's culture iceberg.
GPTs: steam (1784), electricity (1870), automation/internet (1969), now AA/AI; technology grows exponentially, organizations linearly → an exponential gap.
Intangibles went from 17% of S&P 500 market value in 1975 to 92% in 2025; leading tech firms trade at roughly 17–46× book value.
AI stack (chips → cloud → model labs → customers): suppliers finance their own demand, echoing Cisco's vendor lending before funding stopped in 2001.
Models are commoditizing; a deployment layer (DeployCos, forward-deployed engineers) is emerging. Cisco built the network in 3 years; use took 25 to catch up.
Organizations want T-shaped 'generalizing specialists': deep in analytics, broad in strategy, business model, operating model and change management.

topics.x: The grade rests on attendance and participation, a ~1,500-word team paper (teams of 5–6, due before November 9) and a November 17 final pitch to decision-makers that shows the value of an AA/AI initiative and proposes a change-management plan. The five key messages: AI mainstreams models and shifts value to data; impact requires a change in mindset/representations; data creates value as data-for-products/services and products/services-for-data; this reshapes strategy, business and operating models and must be led as change; analytics leaders are best placed to lead it.

Ackoff (1989) ranks data (symbols), information (descriptions: who, what, when, where, how many), knowledge (instructions: how to), understanding (explanations: why) and wisdom (judgment: which ends are worth pursuing), contrasting efficiency (doing things right) with effectiveness (doing the right things). Hausmann splits productive knowledge into tools, explicit knowledge (codes, manuals, formulas, algorithms; instantly transferable at zero cost) and tacit know-how (the ability to perform a task, hard to transfer with cognitive tools alone). Schein's culture iceberg and Nonaka's knowledge-creation work carry this into organizations, and the class asks whether interacting with GenAI is a form of socialization.

topics.n: General-purpose technologies and the exponential gap
topics.x: GPTs are key technologies that shape an era through pervasive use across many sectors and technological dynamism (Bresnahan & Trajtenberg, 1995): steam (1784), electricity (1870), automation and the internet (1969), and now AA/AI with fusion and the convergence of physical, bio and digital technologies. Feedback loops such as Moore's law (transistors per chip double roughly every two years) make technology grow exponentially while organizations change linearly, which opens an exponential gap.

topics.n: Value shift to intangibles and the digital mindset
topics.x: The digital/AI mindset rests on different assumptions: value in intangibles, flywheels and exponentiality, network effects, near-zero marginal cost and a weaker richness-vs-reach trade-off. Market capitalization shows the shift: in September 2026 the ten largest firms, led by NVIDIA at about $5.3T, are almost all technology companies, versus a May 2011 list topped at $417B that spanned oil and gas, technology, finance and mining. Intangibles rose from 17% of S&P 500 market value in 1975 to 92% in 2025, and leading firms trade at 17–46× book value.

topics.n: The AI investment cycle and the deployment layer
topics.x: As Cisco did in the 1990s (lending $2.4B to carriers and dot-coms that bought its routers, until funding stopped in 2001), NVIDIA commits $110B to customers who buy its GPUs, partly on GPU-backed debt. Across the AI stack, equity flows down from chip designers to clouds and model labs while purchase commitments flow back, which raises the bubble question. With models becoming a commodity, value shifts to deployment: labs and hyperscalers are funding deployment companies and forward-deployed engineers, and Cisco's history (network built in 3 years, 25 years for use to catch up) shows why speeding up adoption is the key challenge.

A mindset is a coherent configuration of assumptions and beliefs that condition decisions, actions and behaviors; firms such as BMW explicitly target a 'digital mindset' in their leadership. Organizations increasingly want T-shaped generalizing specialists who combine depth in advanced analytics with breadth in strategy, business model, operating model and change management, bridging AA/AI tools (ML, deep learning, GenAI, RL, optimization) and classic business tools (Five Forces, value chain, economies of scale, DCF/NPV). Functional fixedness bias shows how fixed representations block new solutions.

topics.n: The electricity lesson: same organization vs new organization
topics.x: Edison built generating stations in Manhattan and London in 1881 and electric motors drove machinery soon after, yet by 1900 less than 5% of US factory mechanical drive power came from electric motors. Factories first swapped the steam engine for a motor and kept the layout (same organization, new technology); value came only when machines were freed from the center and the layout was reorganized around what the technology made possible. In the first industrial revolution production followed energy; in the second, energy followed production.

quiz.q: What is the final presentation in 15.681?
o: A pitch to decision-makers showing the value of an AA/AI initiative plus a change-management plan
A technical demo of a trained model
An individual oral exam on the readings
A poster summarizing one case study
quiz.e: It is a pitch to senior management or investors that demonstrates value and proposes a change-management plan. A model demo misses the course's point that the model alone does not create value.

quiz.q: Which pairing describes the two ways data creates value in this course?
o: Data for products/services and products/services for data
Descriptive and predictive analytics
Structured and unstructured data
Internal and external data
quiz.e: Data for products/services improves today's business model; products/services for data explores and enables new products, services and business models.

quiz.q: A manufacturer uses sensor data to cut scrap in its existing plant without changing what it sells. Which mode of value creation is this?
o: Data for products/services: improving today's business model
Products/services for data: enabling a new business model
Both modes at once, since sensors generate new data
Neither, since no AI model is involved
quiz.e: Using data to improve the current business is data for products/services. Products/services for data means using what products generate to build new offerings or business models, which this example does not do.

quiz.q: In Ackoff's hierarchy, which level answers 'Why?'
o: Understanding
Knowledge
Wisdom
Information
quiz.e: Understanding gives explanations (why). Knowledge gives instructions (how to), and wisdom judges which ends are worth pursuing.

quiz.q: Ackoff contrasts efficiency with effectiveness. Effectiveness means:
o: Doing the right things
Doing things right
Doing things faster
Doing things at lower cost
quiz.e: Effectiveness = doing the right things; efficiency = doing things right. Speed and cost are aspects of efficiency.

quiz.q: Which statement describes tacit know-how in Hausmann's framework?
o: The ability to perform a task; hard to transfer using only cognitive tools
Codes, manuals and algorithms; transferable instantly at zero cost
Physical tools, materials and artefacts
Knowledge that is fully captured in documentation
quiz.e: Know-how is implicit (walking, riding a bike, playing tennis). Instant zero-cost transfer is the property of explicit knowledge such as codes and algorithms.

quiz.q: According to Bresnahan & Trajtenberg, a general-purpose technology is characterized by:
o: Potential for pervasive use across many sectors and technological dynamism
Use concentrated in a single high-margin sector
Control by one dominant firm
Government sponsorship of its development
quiz.e: GPTs shape a whole technological era through pervasive use across sectors and ongoing dynamism, e.g. steam, electricity, automation/internet and now AA/AI.

quiz.q: Under Moore's law (transistors double about every two years), by roughly what factor does transistor count grow over 10 years?
quiz.e: 10 / 2 = 5 doublings, so 2^5 = 32×. 5× confuses the number of doublings with the growth factor, the linear reading of exponential change that the 'exponential gap' slide warns about.

quiz.q: A firm has a book value of $108bn and a market value of $4,920bn. What is its market-to-book ratio?
o: About 46×
About 23×
About 4.6×
About 0.02×
quiz.e: 4,920 / 108 ≈ 45.6, so about 46×. 23× is the other firm on the slide ($5,300bn / $229bn), and 0.02× inverts the ratio.

quiz.q: Firm A: book $87bn, market value $1,450bn, 2025 revenue $95bn. Firm B: book $36bn, market value $54bn, 2025 revenue $187bn. Which statement is correct?
o: A trades at about 15× revenue and B at about 0.3× revenue
A trades at about 17× revenue and B at about 1.5× revenue
B is worth more because it has about twice A's revenue
Both trade at roughly 1× revenue
quiz.e: 1,450 / 95 ≈ 15.3 and 54 / 187 ≈ 0.29. The 17× and 1.5× figures are market-to-book multiples, not revenue multiples; B has more revenue but a far lower valuation, the intangibles gap the slide illustrates.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the underlying assumptions of the digital/AI mindset listed in Class 1?
o: Diminishing returns to scale
Network effects
Marginal cost close to zero
Value in intangibles
quiz.e: The digital mindset assumes value in intangibles, flywheels/exponentiality, network effects, near-zero marginal cost and a weaker richness-vs-reach trade-off. Diminishing returns belong to the tangible economy.

quiz.q: What parallel does the lecture draw between Cisco in the 1990s and NVIDIA today?
o: Both finance customers who then buy their products, booking that as revenue, a loop that breaks if funding stops
Both built a network in 3 years that took 25 years to be used
Both were acquired by hyperscalers
Both cut prices to fight commoditization
quiz.e: Cisco lent $2.4B to carriers and dot-coms that bought its routers until funding stopped in 2001; NVIDIA commits $110B to customers who buy GPUs, partly on GPU-backed debt. The 3-year/25-year point is about deployment speed, a separate lesson.

quiz.q: On the AI-stack slide, how do capital and purchases flow between layers?
o: Equity goes down the stack from chip designers to clouds and model labs, while purchase commitments come back up to the suppliers
Customers fund model labs with equity, and labs buy chips directly with that cash
Purchase commitments flow down the stack and equity flows up
Each layer is financed independently by public markets
quiz.e: The slide title: 'Suppliers finance their own demand: equity goes down the AI stack, purchase commitments come back.' That circularity is what prompts the 'Are we in a bubble?' question.

quiz.q: Why does the lecture add a deployment layer to the AI stack?

Chip supply has become the only bottleneck
Regulators require a separate deployment entity
Frontier labs have stopped training new models
quiz.e: Mistral's CEO calls models 'a commodity' with value in deployment and the capacity to run them; labs and hyperscalers are now funding deployment companies and forward-deployed engineers.

quiz.q: Edison built his first generating stations in 1881. By 1900, what share of US factory mechanical drive power came from electric motors, and roughly when had manufacturers 'finally figured out' how to use electricity?
o: Less than 5% by 1900; around 1930, when the technology was nearly 50 years old
Less than 5% by 1900; around 1905, within 25 years
About half by 1900; around 1930
About half by 1900; around 1910
quiz.e: Under 5% by 1900, about 19 years after the first stations, and manufacturers figured it out once the technology was nearly 50 years old: 1881 + ~50 ≈ 1930. The lag is the productivity paradox the course targets.

quiz.q: A bank plugs an LLM into its existing loan-approval workflow and keeps every role and process step unchanged. In the electrification analogy, this is:
o: Same organization, new technology: a motor swapped in for the steam engine while the old layout stays
New organization, new technology
Before electrification: technology dictates the organization
'Energy follows production'
quiz.e: Swapping the technology into an unchanged layout is the middle stage, which delivered little value. Value came only with a new organization designed around the technology.

quiz.q: Which phrase describes the second industrial revolution (electricity, e.g. the Ford production line)?
o: Energy follows production
Production follows energy
Technology dictates the organization
Production follows data
quiz.e: With steam, production had to cluster around the energy source ('production follows energy'); electricity let energy be delivered wherever the production line needed it.

o: A generalizing specialist: deep in advanced analytics, broad across strategy, business model, operating model and change management
A broad generalist with no deep specialty
A specialist with depth in two technical fields
A manager who delegates all analytics work
quiz.e: The vertical bar is depth (advanced analytics), the horizontal bar is breadth across the business disciplines needed to turn models into value.

written.q: Using the electrification of factories, explain the course's claim that 'what stands between analytics and impact is a change in mindset/representations'. Give the timeline facts, describe the three stages of factory organization, and apply the lesson to a company adopting AI today, using the two ways data creates value.
written.m: Edison built generating stations in Manhattan and London in 1881, sold electricity as a commodity within a year, and electric motors drove machinery a year later. Yet by 1900 less than 5% of US factory mechanical drive power came from electric motors, and manufacturers only figured out how to use the technology when it was nearly 50 years old. The three stages: (1) before electrification, machines are constrained by proximity to the central steam engine, so technology dictates the organization; (2) the electric motor replaces the steam engine but the layout and its logic stay the same (same organization, new technology), which yields little gain; (3) machines are freed from the center and the whole layout reorganizes around what the technology makes possible (new organization, new technology). In short, production stopped following energy and energy began to follow production. AA/AI is a general-purpose technology in the same position: plugging a model into an unchanged process is stage 2. A company should first use data for products/services to improve today's business model, and then rethink its representations to pursue products/services for data, meaning new offerings and business models built on the data its products generate. That requires changing the mindset (the assumptions and beliefs behind decisions), strategy, business model and operating model, led as change management, which is the role of T-shaped analytics professionals.
k: 1881 stations; <5% of drive power by 1900; ~50-year lag
Stage 2: same organization, new technology, little value
Production follows energy → energy follows production
AI as a GPT in stage 2 today
Data for products/services vs products/services for data
Mindset/representation change led as change management

written.q: Is the current AI boom a repeat of Cisco and the dot-com bubble? Using the lecture's evidence, discuss the value shift to intangibles, the vendor-financing loop, the AI stack and the emerging deployment layer, and conclude what this implies for analytics professionals.
written.m: Value shift: intangibles rose from 17% of S&P 500 market value in 1975 to 92% in 2025, and leading firms trade at 17–46× book value; the September 2026 top ten by market cap is led by NVIDIA (~$5.3T) and dominated by technology, versus a May 2011 top ten topped at $417B and spread across oil and gas, technology, finance and mining. Firms with more revenue can be worth far less (e.g. $187bn revenue at $54bn market value versus $95bn revenue at $1,450bn). Vendor financing: Cisco lent $2.4B to carriers and dot-coms that bought its routers, booked the sales as revenue, and the loop broke when funding stopped in 2001. NVIDIA commits $110B to customers who buy GPUs, partly on GPU-backed debt. Across the AI stack equity flows down (chips → cloud → model labs) and purchase commitments flow back, so suppliers finance their own demand, and the lecture asks whether this is a bubble. The deeper Cisco lesson is the time lag: Cisco built the network in 3 years and use took 25 years to catch up. With models becoming a commodity, value is moving to deployment: labs and hyperscalers are funding deployment companies, ecosystems and forward-deployed engineers. Whatever the market does, the binding constraint is adoption, which depends on organizations changing their mindsets, business models and operating models. Analytics professionals who are T-shaped, able to build models and also lead strategy and change, are best placed to close that gap.
k: Cisco $2.4B vendor lending, collapse when funding stopped in 2001
Equity down the stack, purchase commitments back up
3 years to build vs 25 years for use to catch up
Models commoditize; value moves to deployment
Implication: T-shaped professionals who lead change
